name: Gurma
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Beckett, Eleanor. 1974. A linguistic analysis of Gurma. MA thesis, University of British Columbia (Dept. of Linguistics). viii+151 pp. UBC cIRcle, DOI 10.14288/1.0058227 (Fada N'Gurma dialect).
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, p. 32, the paragraph directly under Table 2 'Table of Gurma Phonemes'; Ch. 3, p. 55, section 'The noun tonal patterns'; supporting: p. 14 (Symbolization), p. 144 fn. 1, Appendix 2 p. 148 with fn. 1; stress-marked examples pp. 18-19, 26-28, 58; Table 4 p. 69.
catalog_quote: Phonemic tones are very high /"/, high /'/, mid /-/, low /`/ and rising glide, /ˇ/. Stress occurs on the base syllable of nouns and on the first syllable of verbs. Length is phonemic for each vowel and is indicated by writing the vowel twice. [p. 32] ... Only three tones, very high /"/, high /'/ and mid /-/ occur with the simple nouns. Stress, which always occurs on the base, is not marked. [p. 55] ... stress is not marked as it falls on the base and can be predicted. [p. 144, fn. 1] ... Koelle has generally marked stress on the base of the Gurma words where it falls today, but sometimes elsewhere ... This too may be because of the way the Gurma speaker syllabified. [p. 148]

new_statements.citation: Beckett, Eleanor. 1974. A linguistic analysis of Gurma. MA thesis, University of British Columbia (Department of Linguistics). viii+151 pp.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 (Phonology), p. 32 (PDF page 42), immediately below Table 2 'Table of Gurma Phonemes'; reinforced p. 55 (PDF page 65) in the section on noun tonal patterns
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (161 pp., ABBYY text; extracted text read, no scanned needed) is Eleanor Beckett, A Linguistic Analysis of Gurma, MA thesis, UBC, April 1974. Quotes verified at the stated locators: thesis p.32 = p.42, directly under Table 2 'Table of Gurma Phonemes': 'Phonemic tones are very high /"/, high /'/, mid /-/, low /`/ and rising glide /ˇ/. Stress occurs on the base syllable of nouns and on the first syllable of verbs. Length is phonemic for each vowel and is indicated by writing the vowel twice.' (verbatim; only the scanned rendering of the low and rising-glide diacritics is garbled). Thesis p.55 = p.65, section 'The noun tonal patterns': 'Only three tones, very high /"/, high /'/ and mid /-…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gurma is a tone language (very high, high, mid, low + rising glide) that also has non-contrastive, predictable stress: in nouns stress falls on the 'base' syllable (the lexical root that sits between the noun-class prefix and the class suffix, e.g. o-BA-do 'chief'), and in verbs on the first syllable (verbs lack a class prefix, so this is again the root-initial syllable). Stress conditions vowel allophony (short/very short vowels in unstressed syllables, pp. 36-37) and is not marked in Beckett's transcriptions because it is fully predictable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described for the modern language. In Appendix 2 (pp. 148-149) Beckett reinterprets Koelle's 1854 notation: 'Koelle's length sign really indicates primary stress while his accent indicates secondary stress', and notes Koelle generally marked stress 'on the base of the Gurma words where it falls today', occasionally on the prefix.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress; the only variability noted is Koelle's occasional prefix-stressed 19th-century records, attributed to speaker syllabification (p. 148).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (noun = prefix + base + suffix; verb stem). Source is a 1974 MA thesis on the Fada N'Gurma dialect, based on the author's fieldwork; tone, not stress, is the contrastive prosody. Confidence medium because the statement is brief and no later instrumental or specialist (Rialland, Naba) confirmation was accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Beckett 1974 describes the Fada N'Gurma dialect (Burkina Faso), the central/standard variety of Gourmanchéma [gour1243]; no separate glottocode for the dialect. Tersis 1967 (unopened) describes the Kpana variety in northern Togo.

tone_statements.citation: Naba, Jean-Claude (1991). Le gulmanchema: essai de systématisation (phonologie, tonologie, morphophonologie nominale, système verbal). Bayreuth: Universität Bayreuth, Sprach- und Literaturwissenschaftliche Fakultät. x+282 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Le système tonal du gulmancema (nom vernaculaire du gourma, langue Gur, 400000 locuteurs) … Il s'agit, en fait, d'un système à trois tons “ ä niveaux en terrasses ", donc très proche de celui du yoruba. L'étude des réalisations des tons à l'aide de mingogrammes nous a permis d'arriver à la conclusion que chaque ton se différen—cie des autres par deux traits : une hauteur et un contour mélodique. … Deux traits caractérisent donc chaque ton, et il faut insister sur la fréquence de la présence du trait "contour" même si on pose que celui—ci est redondant.
tone_statements.translation: The tone system of Gulmancema (vernacular name of Gurma, a Gur language, 400,000 speakers) … It is, in fact, a three-tone 'terraced-level' system, thus very close to that of Yoruba. The study of the realisations of the tones with mingograms led us to the conclusion that each tone is differentiated from the others by two features: a height and a melodic contour. … Two features thus characterise each tone, and one must insist on how frequently the 'contour' feature is present even if one posits that it is redundant.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (low, high, mid) in a terraced-level system close to Yoruba's; each tone also has a redundant pitch contour; a tone survives elision of its vowel; raised low marks possession.
